entries.title: The 4 Best Planners of 2027: Roterunner, Hobonichi, Cloth & Paper
entries.summary: If digital calendars are leaving you lacking, these WIRED-tested paper agendas and notebooks could change your life.
entries.content:
There’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-new planner, and I've found the best planners if you're shopping for something new for 2027. Whether you're looking to get a little more organized or just love having somewhere to write everything down, the beginning of the year is a great time for a fresh start, and most planner companies have their 2027 planner designs already available.

The world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand. But there's a wide world of options out there that can perfectly suit your needs, especially if you're willing to build your own travel notebook or write in the dates on an undated paper planner, or open to trying your first Japanese-style planner.

After years of testing and a constant stack of planners on my desk, I've found these standout favorite planner styles that could benefit everyone. If you're looking for a tech companion to your paper planner, check out my guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars and Best Digital Notebooks to help keep your calendar and thoughts organized digitally.

Updated November 2026: I've updated the information in this guide to reflect planner availability as 2026 comes to an end and 2027 designs become available. I'm also currently testing 2027 designs from Plum Paper, Laurel Denise, My PA Planner, and Sterling Ink, plus an undated design of Aura Estelle if you're looking for a planner you can start using in December 2026 into the new year.

The Best Planners

If you need a single planner that can do it all and won't burn through your back-to-school budget, this is the one. The Roterunner Purpose Planner is an undated planner that has monthly spreads, weekly spreads, and two full open pages for each week, so there's plenty of room to write longer lists or a project brainstorm. Each monthly and weekly spread has a ton of premade checklist sections for you to use, too. There's even space to track your meals, water intake, and gratitude. It's a planner that actually helps me stay organized and gives me space to track and take notes without running out of room.

The undated nature makes it easy to pick up anytime and use for whichever months you need. Fell off the boat for a few months? No problem. No pages will go to waste when you can fill them in as you go. It only covers six months, but I actually like that; it once again feels like a feasible commitment, especially if you're waffling on how much paper planner you want to promise to use. I love the massive B5 size ($35) since it's finally enough space for me and all my various to-do lists and brainstorms, but there's also a smaller (and cheaper!) A5 ($28) size. It's truly my go-to planner since it has so much space for me to both use the pre-made lists and the open space to actually stay organized and put all my ideas, plans, and notes into one planner. Most others make me feel like I need a companion notebook, but not the Roterunner.

The covers come in a variety of simple colors, and in both hard cover or soft, but the butter-soft faux leather soft cover is my favorite of the bunch. Get it in B5 size if you're always looking for more room in your journals and planners—you won't regret it.

If you're getting into planners, there's no way you won't hear about Hobonichi at some point. There are a few different planners the brand makes, with the Techo being the most popular model. I tested the similar Hobonichi Cousin, which adds weekly spreads to the front of the planner after the monthly overviews. While I don't typically prefer a daily planner style, I was surprised by how much I liked using the Hobonichi. All of Hobonichi's planners use Tomoe River S paper, which is super thin but won't bleed through to the other side. It's also super smooth to the touch and to write on. I liked adding my own structure to the daily pages; I sketched a box to separate my to-do lists and habit trackers from my hourly agenda for the day, and then would usually freeform the rest of the page based on what was on my mind. The Cousin I tested and photographed is an A5 size, while the standard Techo is the smaller A6.

Hobonichi's 2027 editions are here, so you can stock up on your planner for next year right now, plus tons of colors, covers, and other accessories, some of which are unique to 2027. I recommend picking out a protective cover since I did ding up my soft cover quite a bit, and that was just from being used around the house with an occasional trip in a bag. There are little quotes in the corners, but I got a Japanese version instead of an English one, so I can't actually read mine. But honestly, I'm glad I did; I prefer the Japanese lettering to English words on the corners of each page.

I've been obsessed with travel notebooks this year. A travel notebook uses bands to connect three or four notebooks together, and I love using this system to build a customized planner designed for my exact needs. It makes it easy to change the design, too, since you can just switch out a single notebook when it's full.

I really like Cloth & Paper's Travel Notebook Collection. There are 13 different notebooks you can choose from to include in your travel notebook, ranging from classic weekly and monthly spreads to more unique options like a daily wellness notebook and a task planner. It's really a great option if you want a couple of specific things, or even just a regular monthly and weekly notebook plus a blank notebook in the back you can fill with to-do lists and replace anytime without needing an entirely new planner. It's great for students, too, because you can have a notebook dedicated to tracking your assignments and syllabus for the semester. You'll need to create your own, though, as Cloth & Paper doesn't have a dedicated academic notebook for you to select.

I tried both the A5 Slim and the Pocket Plus size, and I really prefer the A5 Slim for a traditional planner experience. The Pocket Plus would be fun to bring on a trip; I wish I'd had it on my latest trip to store little mementos and important things like parking receipts, and could have also written out notes and the plan for the week-long trip. But otherwise, the larger A5 slim was much easier to write on and use for my daily notes and planning.

You'll want the Clear Vinyl Travel Notebook Cover ($23 to $25) no matter which size you choose, which includes elastic bindings to bring all the notebooks you buy together, and you can also pick up more colorful elastic options to add a little more personality to your planner.

I've heard a lot of good things about Erin Condren. Founded in 2005 by Erin Condren, it's known for the LifePlanner that's full of various spreads and productivity tools that you can customize, but there are other variations of planners you can find from the brand. While you'll usually customize your Erin Condren planner if you shop directly on the site, there's a predesigned Target line you can shop that won't give you options, but will give you a well-made planner that's ready to go immediately.

I've been testing the Erin Condren Academic Planner you'll find at Target, but it's sold out as we head into the new year; Erin Condren's website has similar, but more expensive options with more cover and customization options. This base version from Target is a great fit for students and people with deadline-style or client-based work they want to organize. Each month has two pages following the monthly spread to set your most important to-dos and dates, but also a full page to track the month's deadlines and what class (or client, or in my case, story beat) they're for. After that, there are weekly spreads with long columns for each day, and seven blocks of four lines that you can label with things like specific classes, clubs, or organizations, or parenting and household tasks, as I track. It's been a really easy planner to add into my lifestyle, even though it's made for students. There's a class tracker in the front of the planner, too, which I skipped using, plus a detailed holiday calendar, and the back has project and exam pages, plus blank note pages, and even a simple sheet of stickers with things like “Exam,” “Midterm,” and “Paper Due.”

Academic planners usually start in August, so you probably don't want a planner like this if you want something fresh for the new year. But it's still my favorite I've tried if it's your preferred style. Erin Condren does have annual layouts and its popular LifePlanner designs available in 2027 layouts, and other specific designs like budget planners and teacher lesson planners if you're looking for something specific, too.

Honorable Mentions

Like I said, there's a huge world of planners out there. Here are a few that the Reviews team and I at WIRED have tested and enjoyed.

More Planners I’ve Tried

Agendio Basic Planner starting at $48: This is a completely customizable planner. I liked it, and you have the option to design your own pages, and the folder-style cover will protect both the pages and binding. I didn't love the customization tools or abilities as much as I wanted to, and there are a lot of steps to create your planner. I preferred the custom tools of Plum Paper over it. It's a good planner if the pages and binder-style are what you're looking for, and you can find some preset options that usually start around $48 for the smallest page size and black-and-white print.

Ban.do 12-Month Planner for $20: If you're looking for another affordable option but want something with more personality than the Roterunner above, Ban.do's planners are fun and colorful and even come with a page of stickers. It's only a horizontal weekly format, though, which I don't love (but maybe you do!) and the 2027 12-Month designs are now available.

Happy Planner 12-Month Planner for $33: Happy Planner uses disc-bound planners to make it easy to remove and add pages or covers, which is nice for customizability. But they're a very specific aesthetic, and personally, I didn't love turning pages on the discs. Still, it's a good planner if you like the style, and they come in a ton of different layouts. Right now, you can get a Happy Planner that starts in July 2026 and will run you until June 2027, perfect for tracking the academic year.

Laurel Denise Nancy Academic Planner for $44: These planners are cool because you'll look at the month and your weekly at the same time, as the slim weekly pages lay on top of the monthly spread. However, I write way, way too much for the space in these planners, at least for the Nancy design I tested previously. It's great if you just want to write a couple to-dos and meetings per day, but if you want space for detailed lists, you might feel the way I did. I'm currently testing the 2027 Luna ($62) and Scout ($62) planners from Laurel Denise to see if I still feel the same way compared to the original design.

Leuchtturm1917 12-Month Ruled Planner for $29: This is a solid, minimalist planner that has a popular following. It's a simple horizontal weekly layout with the week on one side and a lined page on the other. It's not enough space for everything I write down, but if you're looking for something simple and space for a couple of lists or notes for each week that fit onto a page, it's a good option for you. Leuchtturm1917 also has a nice line of notebooks that look the same from the outside cover, so make sure you actually get the planner.

Muji Undated Weekly Planner for $7: If you want a super simple, super affordable planner, the Muji Undated Weekly is for you. It's just undated weekly horizontal spreads from front to back, even on the paper cover. It's slim, but still more than a year's worth of weeks in it. It's the most minimalist planner I've tried, and though I'm not a fan of horizontal weekly spreads for my planner needs, it's a great cheap option for a lot of people.

Papier Hardcover 2027 Planner for $40: My favorite thing about Papier's planners is how gorgeous the covers are. Papier has a range of beautiful designs you can choose that feel like they belong on a bookshelf rather than just my planner. I tested one of the annual planners, which has the horizontal weekly layout I don't love on any planner (and you can still get that by choosing the mid-year layout for any cover Papier has if you love that style), but the academic one ($29) has a vertical layout that's much more up my alley. Whichever style you like, you can pick. Papier also has softcover academic planners ($32) that use a ring binding, which is easier to lay open than the hard cover binding, and still has both mid-year and academic layout options.

Passion Planner 2027 Planner for $50: This planner was really popular when I was in college, and maybe it still is with the college kids. I liked it, but I feel like the Purpose Planner does a similar thing but better, at least for my needs. It's got vertical spread, but every slot is timed, so I can't use it as a to-do list. It's great for anyone needing to plan out a super detailed schedule and has some to-do list spaces on the bottom, but they're pretty small in my opinion to work for an entire week. It's good for students who only want to track their busy schedules and a couple assignments and tasks for each week.

Some Planner Accessories

Looking for what to pair with your planner? Here are some of our team's favorite daily tools and planner accessories.

Passion Planner Passion Highlighters for $20: If your planner could use a little color, I really like Passion Planner's highlighter sets. They're nice and thin-tipped to fit into slim planner lines, and I especially like the vintage colors for adding color without it feeling neon-bright. You can use the highlighters to organize your plans by type (I like to do red for work, blue for my kid, yellow for things like doctor's appointments, and green for my social life) or color-code your class subjects like we used to do with ringed notebooks.

Pilot Metropolitan Fountain Pen for $34: I never understood the appeal of a fountain pen until I bought one. A properly smoothed fountain pen nib requires very little pressure to write with and seems to glide across the page with a soft, satisfying scratching sound. I know, I'm one of those people now. Much of my initial skepticism came from the perceived complexity of caring for and using a fountain pen, which is very much overblown. My favorite pen of the dozen I've tested is the Pilot Metropolitan with the fine nib. It's easy to work with, taking either prefilled ink cartridges, which you can pop in and out without ever spilling any ink, or you can fill it yourself using a converter and the ink of your choice. I started off using the cartridges, but eventually my quest for a waterproof ink led me to the converter and this sketching ink. Once a week or so, I dip the Metropolitan nib in the bottle of ink and twist the converter to fill the chamber with ink—that's all there is to it. Whichever fountain pen you find works best for you, you’ll find you'll have a quite simply better writing experience. —Scott Gilbertson

Plum Paper Seasonal Stickers for $10: There are a lot of stickers out there you could use for your planners, but my favorites—especially for the holidays—are from Plum Paper. They're beautiful and fun, and are mostly nice and small to fit into small lines or monthly charts without eating up the entire section. I like that there's a mix of shapes and styles, and you can also shop stickers for themes like home, fitness, wellness, and baby milestones. You can even make your own custom stickers (starting at $12), which are only thick line-style stickers where you can customize the word and icon on them. Still, very handy!

Planner Alternatives

Not everyone needs or wants a rigid planner. If you just need daily to-do lists or are a fan of bullet journals, consider getting a great notebook instead.

Maybe you just want a plain, lined notebook. One of our former reviewers recommended the Midori MD Notebook, and I found it to be a nice small size if you're looking for something minimal. It comes in lined, unlined, or dot-grid, and uses paper made from cotton pulp (just like money!) Midori’s notebooks are designed to fit inside notebook or journal covers (which you can find all over Etsy). The pages are a subtle off-white and have a weight and texture that draw you in.

One of our reviewers skips a planner entirely and instead writes down his to-do list on a 3-by-5 index card. He puts that index card into his pocket with a pocket-sized memo book like this one from Field Notes ($13 for three), where he jots down notes throughout the day to use for the next day's to-do list. Both the notebook and index cards fit inside a waxed canvas notebook cover to keep them safe from the elements (or just his pocket). It's an affordable and easy-to-manage system.

FAQs

Why Choose a Paper Planner?

Studies show that it's good for your brain to write things down. Sure, you could put your calendar in an online tool, but putting pen to paper activates more brain connectivity. We're more likely to remember and learn things if we write them down by hand, so using a paper planner for your to-do list can make it easier to remember. Plus, it's fun! You're given a creative space to let out everything you need to remember, from appointments to the day's tasks, and customize it in a way that best helps you stay organized.

What Style Paper Planner Is Best for You?

Paper planners mainly come in two styles: weekly and daily. Daily planners have an entire page dedicated to each day, while weekly planners have an entire week spread across just two pages. These aren't the only options (monthly is another popular one, for example, but not as popular as these two styles), but they're the most common you'll see. I like daily planners for folks who have a really busy schedule they want to plan out, and long daily to-do lists. Weekly planners are great if you want to be able to write down a few things per day but don't need an entire page.

What Sizes Do Planners Come In?

Here are a couple common planner sizes. My favorite are the larger sizes since I like lots of room to doodle, but the smaller A5 is a popular choice for a book-sized planner that won't take up too much space. Not all paper planners use the same sizing names—Moleskine, for example, calls its A5 size a large—so you'll want to check measurements before you purchase.

  • A5 (5.8 by 8.3 inches)
  • Regular/Medium / B5 (7 by 9 inches)
  • Large/Letter (8.5 by 11 inches)
  • Personal/Pocket (3.5 by 5.5 inches)

entries.title: AI DJs Completely Kill My Groove
entries.summary: YouTube Music and Spotify want synthetic hosts to curate your playlists. Their awkward banter and bogus song trivia are ruining the vibe.
entries.content:
I usually can’t pinpoint the moment I stop using a software feature, with most tools drifting out of fashion without an expiration date. That’s not the case with YouTube Music’s “Beyond the Beat,” an AI-generated DJ that explains songs to you.

YouTube Music is my music-streaming service of choice. And since I’m a software reporter, I always enable the beta features available through YouTube Labs, which include Beyond the Beat. YouTube’s AI DJ randomly interjects for about 30 seconds between songs, teeing up the vibe shift and providing context about the next track.

More listeners are encountering synthetic commentary built into their music streaming apps. While YouTube launched this experimental AI DJ in 2025, Spotify first introduced a similar tool back in 2023. It doubled down on its AI DJ efforts in November, expanding the different personalities available to users and adding more controls over the commentary.

These AI DJs aren’t just annoying. Their attempts to provide helpful context and mimic human candor ultimately fall flat. Lucky for me, both features are optional and avoidable.

After months of leaving it enabled, a bad experience with Beyond the Beat this week pushed me to swear off AI DJs altogether. I was listening to a pop divas playlist as part of my morning workout and got slapped with 30 seconds of exposition after a Slayyyter track:

“Hey Boy delivers that high-energy surge perfectly, but we're shifting our focus to a sharper, more visceral reality. In Rock Music, Charli XXC [sic] weaves in a biting, dark sense of humor regarding the physical toll of her relentless 2024 and 2025 touring. She turns the genuine nerve damage she sustained on the road into a strange sort of battle scar, reclaiming the exhaustion of a weary party girl as a badge of honor. It's an unflinching look at the cost behind the spectacle, where the grind of the industry becomes the actual subject matter. Here is Rock Music by Charli XXC [sic].”

What a lengthy paragraph of platitudes with little substance. That’s not even mentioning how the AI DJ butchered the pronunciation of a little-known, indie act called Charli XCX. This flub reflected my overall experience with YouTube Music’s AI DJ. It took me out of the groove and didn’t feel additive.

In another example, it went in-depth on the meaning of Olivia Rodrigo’s Expectations remix featuring Chappell Roan, calling it a "structural interpretation” that unpacks the “nuances of queer dating.” Then YouTube Music played the original track, sans Roan; so much for the queer yearning.

Curious how Spotify’s AI DJ experience would compare, I upgraded my account to the premium tier for access to that beta software. One of the biggest recent changes to Spotify’s AI DJ was adding new voices to the lineup, so I went into my settings and played the introduction clips for each of the eight English-language voices.

Maybe I was already a bit miffed from my YouTube Music experience because these voices immediately started to frustrate me. Multiple voices leaned into filler words such as “you know” and “like,” as the AI described the next songs it would play. Knowing an AI voice is being trained to use filler words to sound more human gave me the uncanny-valley ick.

Spotify’s AI DJ was fairly different from YouTube Music’s version. On Spotify, the AI DJ is also an algorithmically guided experience that picks songs for you based on past listening habits and song requests. Overall, Spotify’s synthetic commentary felt tighter and more tolerable than YouTube’s blabbering DJ. That said, neither software experience was enjoyable enough for me to return.

Although Spotify claims it has “80 percent of listeners coming back to DJ week after week,” according to the company’s launch blog, I won’t be one of them. My rejection of AI DJs isn’t based on how they audibly sound. The voices, from both companies, are decent and sound convincingly human. The content of their commentary is what truly turns me off. Whether it’s empty platitudes or mimicking human mistakes, I’ve heard enough.

entries.title: Evercade Nexus Review: The Best Retro Handheld Yet
entries.summary: Evercade’s best handheld yet is a major level-up for the retro specialist.
entries.content:
Excellent design feels more like a “real” handheld console. Improved battery life. Bright, colorful, smooth screen. Thumbsticks pave the way for even more retro games.

TIRED

No meaningful, powerful boost to previous Evercades. No more HDMI out. D-pad sits too high.

Specialist hardware manufacturer Blaze Entertainment has spent the 2020s quietly carving out a niche for itself as the go-to option for retro gaming. With a stable of reliable hardware, from the original Evercade handheld to the Evercade Alpha bartop arcade cabinet, it offers numerous ways to play, all built around an ever-expanding library of physical cartridges. Each brings a curated selection of classic titles and lost curiosities to modern players.

The Evercade Nexus is more than just the latest addition to its console lineup. While it retains compatibility with every previously released Evercade cartridge, it’s also the biggest leap forward the line has taken so far, both in hardware and in what it might offer with games going forward. It’s a real level up—and it’s rather brilliant.

Bigger and Better

The most obvious change is the sheer size. Where Blaze’s previous handhelds were about on par with the original Game Boy Advance, aimed at pocketable play, the Evercade Nexus is closer in scale to a Nintendo Switch Lite. It measures 215 x 111 x 34 millimeters and weighs 410 grams—still easily portable, but more in the “buy a protective hard case and throw it in your bag” kind of way.

The size increase works in its favor, though. The larger design feels more substantial, with more real estate for your hands for better comfort. The control layout remains broadly the same as the Evercade EXP—a D-pad, ABXY face buttons, shoulder buttons, and triggers all return, with a few beneficial tweaks. Notably, the triggers are now chunkier and curved to meet your fingers, while all four shoulder inputs and the rear of the device are now nicely textured for better grip.

The big change is the addition of twin symmetrical thumbsticks. This has implications for Evercade going forward—more on that later—but it also improves Tate Mode (pronounced tah-tay, meaning vertical in Japanese), a returning feature from the Evercade EXP. As on that model, tapping the dedicated mode-shift button rotates the screen 90 degrees, letting you play vertically scrolling arcade games in the intended orientation, rather than crammed into a tiny pillar-boxed view on the widescreen display.

On the EXP, you’d hold the console on the left to use the D-pad for movement, which required duplicate A+B buttons on that side and cluttered the inputs. On the Nexus, Tate Mode rotates in the opposite direction, letting you use the right-hand thumbstick and the default ABXY buttons. It feels much better—again aided by the increased overall size—and keeps the device's design looking much tidier.

Whichever orientation you play in, the screen is bigger—a 5.89-inch IPS panel with an 840 × 512-pixel resolution for a 167 pixels-per-inch density, versus the original's 4.3-inch LCD—and brighter, now boasting 500-plus nits. It’s clear and colorful, and games look fantastic on it.

The only minor build-quality demerits are the D-pad, which feels a little too raised and prone to rocking—a slightly more flush fit would have been better—and the glossy finish under the face buttons and around the front trim. These accents are aesthetically pleasing, standing out from the matte plastic of the rest of the unit, but they attract micro-scratches far too easily. Those small gripes aside, the Nexus is a huge improvement on its predecessors, feeling less like a quirky gadget and more like a serious, modern gaming handheld.

Up and Downgrades

The Nexus doesn’t actually see any boosts in processor power or memory. It still uses the 1.5-GHz quad-core chip in the EXP with 512 MB of RAM. That may not sound like much in 2026, but it’s significantly more powerful than the original hardware it emulates, and it ensures Evercade’s universal cross-device compatibility for every cartridge.

The downside is that the Nexus still feels slow at the system level. Booting it up takes about 35 to 40 seconds on average, and it can take about the same to load up a cartridge. Games don't have any performance issues, but getting there is sluggish. Disappointingly, there’s also no quick-suspend feature, forcing you to power off fully and back on between play sessions.

There are some upgrades to the underlying tech, though. One material improvement is the battery, which jumped to a 5,000-mAh cell from the EXP's 3,000 mAh. Even with that bigger, brighter screen sucking up juice, the Nexus offers around five hours of play between charges, roughly an hour longer. On the audio front, the integrated front-facing stereo speakers are solid, offering louder, clearer output. Even better, the Nexus now supports Bluetooth, finally allowing you to connect wireless headphones, while still offering a 3.5-mm jack for wired headsets.

Bluetooth isn’t the only connectivity upgrade. The Nexus now supports the Wi-Fi 6 standard and can connect to 5-GHz networks (previous models could only use slower 2.4-GHz ones). That’s useful for downloading console updates and Evercade’s free Game of the Month. It also enables the new EverSync feature, unique to the Nexus, which allows multiple units to communicate wirelessly. Much like Nintendo’s GameShare, it’s set to allow multiplayer across devices even with only one cartridge, although I haven't been able to test this feature yet.

The underlying OS also gets a refresh. Hop into the settings menu and you'll find new customization tools. These let you adjust the color palette for the menu background and the glowing LED Nexus logo, select onscreen borders for non-widescreen games, and even tweak aspect ratios and virtual scan lines—all nice ways to personalize your device.

The glaring omission is any form of TV connectivity. Previous handheld Evercades featured a mini-HDMI out port, but that’s removed entirely here. It was always a nice-to-have rather than a major selling point, but it’s disappointing to lose a feature. Evercade players wanting TV play will have to opt for the Evercade VS-R set-top console.

A New Era for Old Games

While the Nexus hardware is a significant improvement, more exciting is where the games themselves may be heading. Almost every game on Evercade to date has been from the 8-bit or 16-bit era, if not earlier, a period that near-universally consisted of 2D titles. Adding thumbsticks opens the door to an entirely new generation of 3D games. Blaze says the Nexus works with 32- and 64-bit games, which dramatically expands possibilities for future releases.

More impressively, the first two cartridges to benefit from this generational leap also see Evercade step beyond emulation for the first time. Both the Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie double-pack and the DOOM and DOOM II collection are natively ported. That means improved performance, intentional widescreen aspect ratios to match the display, higher resolutions up to 60 frames per second, and on-cartridge save slots rather than virtual quick saves.

The Banjo duology is the real standout so far, with the colorful worlds of Rare’s classic 3D platformers shining on the Nexus’ superior screen while taking full advantage of the dual thumbsticks (something the N64 controller lacked) to offer smoother camera controls alongside free movement. These are authentic and accessible versions of 64-bit gaming greatness, without compromise. This might be the best way to play this pair of games, period, and all the better for being able to do so portably. (For anyone who’s looked up the price of a Banjo-Tooie cart on the secondary market, a bargain, too.) The DOOM collection also holds up well, with classic boomer shooters and a stack of bonus missions and map packs, but as some of the oldest examples of first-person shooters, they show their age more.

The ports are to Evercade as an ecosystem, meaning the cartridges will still play on existing hardware—even Blaze’s budget Super Pocket devices—with camera controls mapped to shoulder buttons, albeit with a slower rotational view. It also partly explains the lack of power upgrades for the Nexus, as cross-device compatibility is a signature of the collection. Still, as Blaze works its way through gaming history, it feels as though a future Evercade will inevitably have to make a break to offer more power and support more recent games.

For now, though, the Nexus is hands-down the best way to play both Evercade’s vast library of games and this new pseudo-generation of native releases. With its better screen, bigger form, and added controls for 3D games, it’s a delight to play on. If Blaze can keep up the momentum with more dedicated ports, this will be a bright new age for the best old games.

entries.title: Logitech Yeti 2 Review: An All-In-One Studio Setup
entries.summary: The follow-up to the iconic Yeti microphone is here, and its upgrades make it worthy of the legacy.
entries.content:
The original Blue Yeti microphone was first released in 2009, and it remains the most ubiquitous microphone for home recording 17 years later. Chances are, if you’ve watched a YouTube video, Twitch stream, or listened to a podcast, you’ve heard (and probably seen) this microphone at least once.

Long after absorbing Blue and phasing out the brand name, Logitech has finally released its highly anticipated successor: the Yeti 2. The follow-up maintains the same general shape and look but drastically changes the microphone’s functionality. Instead of simply recording audio, the Yeti 2 has a handful of features to monitor and manipulate the audio passing through it, seamlessly recording production-quality audio with zero delay. While some of the design feels a bit underdeveloped, the Yeti 2 is a deserving sequel to the iconic original model and an easy shoe-in as the best USB microphone you can buy.

Intuitive Interfaces

The Yeti 2's biggest upgrades stares you directly in the face after taking it out of the box. The built-in screen and dial allow for on-the-fly adjustments right on the microphone. No software required. While I was a skeptic at first, I quickly found this little screen to be significantly more convenient than the alternative. It can be used to adjust gain, enable different post-processing settings, and configure the sound profile of the microphone.

More importantly, the screen can quickly provide insights into audio quality at a glance. The main screen shows a graph of the gain-adjusted input volume, which is what the microphone is sending to your computer. It can also display a histogram of volume over time, a pattern to show what direction input is coming from, or … a pixel-art Yeti. This little guy looks confused when you’re quiet, happy when you’re talking at a normal volume, and alarmed when you’re too loud for the microphone to handle. Within the G Hub app, the icons can be swapped out with any of Logi’s other premade avatars (a dragon, flower, frog, or jellyfish), or freely customized with your own images using a simple drag-and-drop menu. This is the least functional feature of the microphone, but it’s an endearing and intuitive way to indicate audio quality at a glance.

The screen also has quite a few adjustable menus for different features, including a de-noise function with four levels, five EQ presets, a pattern customizer with eight default options, and a multitude of toggleable settings to clean up and improve recording quality. While the settings can’t be customized using the screen, the G Hub application provides more in-depth adjustments for how intense each of these settings are, along with explanations of how they work and when to use them.

entries.title: This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets
entries.summary: A Carnegie Mellon student’s tiny E Ink gadgets, called OATs, give houseplants, skateboards, and dumbbells expressive personalities to nudge you toward better habits.
entries.content:
You forgot to water the plant. Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected. Maybe that'll give you the push you needed to grab the watering can. As you pour water into the soil, the plant pet on the screen gets excited and happy.

That's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects. The tech was created by Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student in Carnegie Mellon's Future Interfaces Group. Kim presented the project at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in Detroit in early November, a forum where academics and industry experts explore human-computer interfaces, and she earned two Honorable Mention awards.

You might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ’90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention. Kim’s goal was to bring a similar experience to physical objects in our lives. “We bring this joy of caring from virtual to physical objects,” she tells WIRED. While folks have encouraged Kim to sell OAT kits online, she hasn't decided whether to pursue it as a business opportunity.

Kim says everyone spends all day staring at mobile devices, and AI agents—even if they're designed to handle tasks on your behalf—still demand attention from your smartphone screen. OATs were a way to bring those interactions out into the real world.

Giving AI a physical body isn't new, as companies rush to create “the next smartphone,” whether that's failed attempts like the Humane Ai Pin, OpenAI's upcoming hardware created in collaboration with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, or Meta's Muse Charm. The pocket-sized gadget houses Meta's popular Muse AI agent and is expected to launch in December. Increasingly, though, companies have leaned on “cuteness” in their strategy for widespread adoption.

OATs have an E Ink display connected to internal and external sensors that can track things like moisture, temperature, humidity, light, occupancy, and motion. (The hardware is relatively cheap, around $20 for the main module.) The sprites are created with Google Gemini's Nano Banana image-generation service, creating a suite of emotions for various states based on the sensor data. You can set all of this up through a web portal, where you can name your OAT and choose which sensors to use for the object you're attaching it to.

The web app will generate “Positive” and “Negative” behaviors based on your object's name and description. So if the OAT is attached to a plant, positive triggers could be “consistent air temperature readings” and “low humidity levels” if the plant of choice prefers dry environments. However, you can customize these behaviors to suit your specific plant type.

It can be used for very simple things. Want to use your skateboard more often? Attach the OAT to your board, and if it hasn't detected motion for a few days, the avatar will look sad and lonely. You don't want that, do you? As Kim says, “These kinds of inanimate objects can be more expressive.” When you hop on the board, the OAT avatar will be happy, with fun faces.

The catch is that the system's battery life is really short, showing why this is more of a proof of concept than anything else. OATs last around three to four days, but paired with the sound-level sensor, they'll only last a day. It has a USB-C port for charging the lithium-ion polymer battery.

Kim says she distributed OATs to many people and found that they used them in three different ways. One is, “Am I being used?” Like when you attach an OAT to a coffee machine and have the avatar get excited when the machine starts grinding beans. The second is for warning people near an object. For example, 3D printers release toxic fumes during use, and attaching an OAT to one can warn people that the device is operational. And the third is to track their own behaviors. Someone attached an OAT to a dumbbell to track how often they lifted weights, encouraging themselves to exercise regularly so they wouldn't disappoint the AI pet.

The demo at the symposium was popular, and Kim turned it into a competition to see who could come up with the most interesting ideas about what objects to pair with the OATs. Kim's website features a gallery with sprites people made, from an animated conference badge to a panda avatar for an Owala water bottle.

But the demo also ignited a huge discussion about anthropomorphizing artificial intelligence, and whether it’s proper to give these sprites humanlike traits and emotions to make people feel connected with them.

It's already a topic in play within the AI industry. Companies often refer to their chatbot behaviors in human terms, like when they “hallucinate.” Anthropic announced a “dreaming” feature this summer where its AI agent cleaned up its local memory as a background process. These anthropomorphized terms can distort moral judgments about AI and cause people to overly trust the tools.

Kim says that's why OATs have very limited interactions, restricted to expressive emotions and the E Ink display.

“Anthropomorphism can be very useful in certain ways, like helping people to change their behaviors,” Kim says. “People name their car, and they name their bike. I rarely see people who name their iPhone. I feel like in the future of computing we will have more of a relationship with AI, but we should definitely be careful not to abuse this."
